title: Security and Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response & Evidence Workflows
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's controls and operational procedures for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC practices, incident response for security incidents, compliance evidence collection workflows, and management of risk & exceptions. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineering, security, and compliance stakeholders.

Scope
- Applies to all Redwood-managed control plane components, public-hosted APIs, Dedicated pools, and Private deployment control planes.
- Excludes customer-managed on-prem model artifacts unless integrated with Redwood control plane services.
- Audience: engineering leads, platform SREs, product security, GRC, and auditors.

Owners and escalation
- Primary owner: Security (owner_team).
- Secondary owners: Eng-Infra (cloud accounts and networking), Eng-SRE (operational tooling).
- Security on-call escalation: follow the incident response playbook; pager duty: security-oncall@redwood (see related playbook).

1) RBAC and Authentication
Purpose: Provide least-privilege access to control plane APIs, consoles, and production telemetry.
Standards:
- Identity providers: Okta for SSO; SCIM provisioning into our IAM service.
- Authentication: OIDC for web/console, OAuth2 bearer tokens for service-to-service, mutual TLS for inter-service where possible.
- Authorization model: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) with scoped permissions and attribute-based policy overlays for sensitive operations.
- Default access: deny. All privileges must be requested via access request workflow and justified in ticket (Jira).

Key roles and examples:
- security-admin: full access to audit logs, evidence artifacts, risk exception approvals. (Restricted to Security team, SLA: 24h approval).
- infra-admin: manage cloud accounts, network, VPC peering. (Requires 2FA, SCIM group membership).
- svc-deployer: can push runtime configuration to Dedicated pools.
- read-only-ops: dashboard & metrics access only.

RBAC Policy lifecycle:
1. Define role and required actions in code (policy-as-code repository: infra/policies/rbac).
2. Review by Security and Eng-Platform.
3. Deploy via CI with automated policy-testing harness.
4. Annual re-certification: owners must review membership.

Sample policy (YAML snippet) included for implementers:
---
role: svc-deployer
permissions:
  - resource: deployment/*
    actions: [create, update, view]
  - resource: metrics/*
    actions: [view]
constraints:
  - attribute: environment
    allowed: [staging, production]
---

Onboarding and offboarding:
- New hire path: request groups via Okta SCIM; automation grants base roles; additional accesses require ticket and manager approval.
- Offboard: SCIM deprovisioning immediately removes console access; service credentials rotated within 24 hours.

2) Audit logging
Purpose: Maintain an immutable, queryable record of security-relevant events to support investigations, compliance (SOC2, ISO27001), and forensics.
Minimum logging requirements:
- Authentication events: login success/failure, token issuance, token revocation.
- Authorization decisions: allow/deny for sensitive API calls (create/delete model, modify routing policy, alter billing bindings).
- Administrative actions: role changes, risk exception approvals, evidence uploads.
- Data access: access to customer data stores, exports, and backups.
- System events: service restarts, configuration changes, deployments to control plane.

Retention and storage:
- Audit log retention default: 3 years for security team (stored in WORM-enabled S3 bucket, encrypted with CMKs).
- Shorter retention (90 days) configurable for non-compliance environments; must be approved by Security and Legal.

Integrity and access:
- Logs are shipped to central SIEM (Splunk/Chronicle) with signed forwarders.
- Integrity: HMAC chain (per-service) to detect tampering; verification run weekly.
- Access: only security-admin and designated incident responders have raw-log read access; others through vetted query dashboards.

Example log schema (single-line JSON example):
{"timestamp": "2027-10-12T15:22:10Z", "service": "control-plane-api", "event": "role.change", "actor": "alice@redwood.com", "target": "svc-deployer", "request_id": "req_12345abc"}

3) Data residency and retention
Policy principles:
- Customers choose residency at onboarding (US, EU, APAC regions).
- Data types: control-plane metadata (minimal), PII, logs, customer-provided prompt/response data. Each type has separate residency and retention options.

Default retention windows:
- Control-plane metadata: 2 years
- Audit logs (security): 3 years (see audit logging)
- Customer prompt/response data: default 30 days; configurable to 0 days (ephemeral) or up to 7 years for enterprise contracts.
- Backups and snapshots: encrypted, region-bound unless cross-region replication is requested and approved.

Implementation notes:
- At-rest encryption: CMKs per-region via KMS; keys are bound to the residency region.
- Data movement: no cross-region copies unless customer opts in and Legal signs Data Transfer Agreement. Cross-region replication must be recorded in evidence workflow.

Deletion and disposition:
1. Customer requests deletion via console or support ticket.
2. Automated deletion job marks data for deletion, then shredding job purges storage and updates evidence record.
3. For forensics/incident holds, deletion can be suspended; holds must be approved by Security and Legal and recorded in evidence workflow.

4) Secure SDLC (Software Development Lifecycle)
Goal: Integrate security controls into each stage of development to reduce vulnerabilities in production-facing systems.
Mandatory gates:
- Design review: threat model and data flow diagram required for new services handling regulated data.
- Code scanning: static analysis (SAST) on PRs, dependency scanning for OSS vulnerabilities (dependabot/WhiteSource).
- Secrets scanning: pre-commit and CI checks; any detected secret triggers immediate rotation and a security ticket.
- Infrastructure as code review: terraform plan must pass policy-as-code tests (OPA/Rego).
- Build and release: reproducible builds, SBOM generated for each release.
- Runtime: runtime security (container image signing, vulnerability scanning).

Security testing cadence:
- Weekly dependency alerts triaged within 5 business days.
- Quarterly internal pentests; annual external pentest for public API and Dedicated offering.
- Fuzzing and chaos experiments for critical path services at least twice per year.

Developer responsibilities:
- PRs must include security checklist: [threat model, data classification, secrets usage].
- Owners must respond to security findings within SLA windows: critical (24h), high (72h), medium (14d), low (quarterly backlog).

CI sample snippet (policy gate):
- name: policy-check
  run: |
    opa test infra/policies || exit 1

5) Incident response – security procedures
Objective: Rapid detection, containment, remediation, and post-incident evidence collection for security incidents affecting Redwood or customer data.
Classification and SLA:
- Incident types: Data breach, Privilege misuse, Infrastructure compromise, Supply-chain compromise, Unauthorized access.
- Initial response SLAs: acknowledge (15 min), initial triage (1 hr), containment plan within 4 hrs for P1 incidents.

Playbook summary (high level):
1. Detection & triage: Security monitoring alerts (SIEM), customer report, or internal detection. Document initial facts in incident ticket and assign incident commander.
2. Containment: Revoke affected tokens/keys, isolate instances, apply network ACLs, rotate credentials.
3. Root cause analysis: gather logs, snapshots, run forensic tools (EBS snapshot of affected host in read-only).
4. Remediation: patch/apply config changes, restore from safe backups, rotate secrets.
5. Communication & disclosure: follow breach notification timelines; coordinate with Legal, Customer Success, and Communications.
6. Post-incident: create postmortem, map findings to action items, verify fixes, and update playbooks.

Forensic evidence collection checklist:
- Preserve logs (export to evidence bucket, do not modify).
- Snapshot affected compute and store hash for chain-of-custody.
- Record all commands executed by responders in incident log.
- Tag evidence set with incident ID and retention policy (default: 7 years for incidents involving customer data).

6) Compliance evidence workflows
Purpose: Provide auditable artifacts for SOC2/ISO/other audits and internal evidence requests.
Evidence types and owners:
- Access reviews: reports of group membership and role approvals (owner: HR/security).
- Audit logs: SIEM exports and integrity proofs (owner: Security).
- Change records: Git commits, PR reviews, and CI artifacts (owner: Eng-Platform).
- Penetration testing reports: vendor reports and remediation tracking (owner: Security).

Workflow steps:
1. Evidence request received (GRC Portal/Jira).
2. Security triages request and assigns appropriate owners.
3. Evidence is exported (signed manifest) to evidence storage (WORM S3) and access is time-limited.
4. Reviewer verifies artifacts and signs off in evidence registry.
5. Request closed and annotated with retention instructions.

Automation and tooling:
- Evidence registry: internal service that tracks evidence exports, signatures, and reviewer approvals.
- Signed manifests created using CMK and stored alongside artifacts.
- Templates provided for auditors to request common evidence sets (SOC2: access controls, change management, incident history).

7) Risk and exceptions management
Principles:
- Exceptions are time-boxed, compensating controls must be documented, and ownership assigned.
- Risk acceptance requires business justification and approval by Security and the relevant product/engineering lead.

Exception request process:
1. Submit exception ticket with: scope, duration, compensating controls, rollback plan, and owner.
2. Security reviews and classifies risk (Low/Medium/High).
3. Approvals: Low — security lead; Medium — security manager + product; High — CISO and legal.
4. Exception tracked in risk register and reviewed at quarterly risk board.

Example compensating controls:
- If audit logging cannot be enabled in a test environment, compensate with time-limited session recordings and scheduled manual exports.
- If cross-region replication is required for availability, require customer consent, DTA, and encrypted transit with key separation.

8) Monitoring and continuous improvement
- Quarterly control review: owners must demonstrate controls meet policy and close outstanding actions.
- Monthly metrics to measure program health: number of open exceptions, time-to-rotate-secrets, mean-time-to-containment for P1 incidents.
- Bi-annual tabletop exercises that include GRC and CS to validate communication and notification flows.

Appendix A — Quick commands and sample artifacts
- Exporting logs for incident:
  aws s3 cp s3://audit-logs/control-plane/2027-10-12/ /tmp/audit-20271012 --recursive --profile security-readonly
- Create evidence manifest (sample):
  {"manifest_id": "evid-20271012-01", "created_by": "security@redwood.com", "items": ["s3://evidence/incident-123/logs.gz"]}
- Sample SIEM query (failed logins > 5 in 10m):
  source=auth_logs | where event=\"login_failure\" | stats count() by user | where count > 5
